name: Hanga
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hanga (hang1258) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Hunt 1988 'Tone and stress analysis by computer' (SIL Notes on Linguistics 41: 14-18), was located as an open archive.org microfiche scan of the 1988 issue run (micro_IA41152957_0648, = ERIC ED340197), downloaded, the article pages extracted, and read in full. It is a report on an SIL-built PC acoustic-analysis board that uses two Hanga recordings as a test case; it states that Hanga has two emic tones plus downdrift and intonation and that the instrument's amplitude trace picked out a low-toned syllable as the most stressed in one utterance, but it gives no rule or statement of where word stress falls in Hanga. Relevance: prosody (tone/instrumental amplitude), not word stress; no catalog record to confirm or contradict; nothing left to acquire from this item. No first-hand word-stress statement for Hanga was obtained in this sweep; the outstanding candidate is Hunt & Hunt 1981 'A phonology of the Hanga language' (HathiTrust search-only; Harvard print), which is not in the sweep list and was not reachable (sil.org and HathiTrust blocked by Cloudflare from our machine

new_statements.quote: The Hanga language is a tonal language, but my own ability to distinguish tone is very limited, which is why this project exists. [p. 14] ... Rosemary and I have analyzed the Hanga language as having two emic tones plus downdrift and intonation tone. [p. 16] ... The relevant syllable is the most stressed syllable in the utterance and, since stress in English (Rosemary's mother tongue) is associated with a relatively high pitch, the stress probably deceived her. ... The downdrift of tone showed up very clearly. A stressed low tone was indicated clearly. [p. 16]
new_statements.citation: Hunt, Geoffrey R. (1988). Tone and stress analysis by computer. Notes on Linguistics 41: 14-18. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: p. 14 (section 1) and p. 16 (section 3, 'Comparison with manually recorded phonetic data'); PDF pages 1 and 3 of the extracted file
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (5 pp., extracted from the archive.org microfiche scan micro_IA41152957_0648 of Notes on Linguistics 41-43, 1988). Rendered PDF pp. 1 and 3 to images and read them: PDF p. 1 carries the printed page number 14 and the title 'TONE AND STRESS ANALYSIS BY COMPUTER by Geoffrey Hunt'; PDF p. 3 carries the running head '16 NOTES ON LINGUISTICS, Number 41, January 1988' and section '3. COMPARISON WITH MANUALLY RECORDED PHONETIC DATA'. All quoted sentences are present verbatim on the page images: p. 14 'The Hanga language is a tonal language, but my own ability to distinguish tone is very limited, which is why this project exists.'; p. 16 'Rosemary and I have analyzed the Hanga language…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hanga is a two-tone language (H, L) with downdrift and intonation. The source gives no rule for word-stress placement: 'stress' is treated only as a phonetic amplitude peak at utterance level, which in the analysed utterance fell on the initial (lengthened, low-toned) syllable of a shortened form of naaba 'chief'. Nothing is said about a fixed or predictable word-stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the note does not describe a stress system at all, only that an amplitude-defined stress peak can coincide with a low tone (so stress does not equal high pitch in Hanga).
new_statements.domain_note: Connected-speech utterances from tape-recorded texts (a narrative and instructions), not citation forms; the remarks concern one utterance. The item is a computer-phonetics note, not a phonological description; the Hunts' actual phonology (Hunt & Hunt 1981) could not be opened.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Hunt 1988 concerns the Hanga of Ghana (Gur, Western Oti-Volta), i.e. hang1258 / ISO hag, fieldwork c. 1971-1981 in the Hanga area (Savannah Region). Not to be confused with Hanga = Oluwanga (Luhya, Kenya, lwg) or Hanga Hundi (PNG, wos), which pollute search results. Glottolog's CLDF tags two Hunt items (the 1981 phonology, ref 72738, and the 1980 WALDS sheet, ref 679311) with [kama1357] Kamara, but the titles and the parallel hh entries (20668, 155185) make clear they describe Hanga.

sources.note: First-hand by the language's principal describer: Hanga 'is a tonal language' (p. 14); 'two emic tones plus downdrift and intonation tone' (p. 16). Stress appears only as an utterance-level amplitude trace: the most-stressed syllable of one utterance was a low-tone syllable ('A stressed low tone was indicated clearly', p. 16). No rule for where word stress falls. Page 16 verified against the page image.
